walkthroughs.body_html:
Cross Tt × Tt (T = tall).

Punnett: TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Genotype 1:2:1; phenotype 3 tall: 1 short. 75% are tall.

Colour-blindness is X-linked recessive. X^B = normal; X^b = colour-blind.

Carrier mum X^B X^b × normal dad X^B Y → 25% chance of a colour-blind son.

If a beneficial allele has frequency 0.1 and rises 0.02 per generation, after 5 generations it is 0.1 + 5 × 0.02 = 0.20.

This is simplified — real selection slows as alleles become common.

mcqs.q: In Tt × Tt, the chance of tt is:
X^B X^b carrier mother × X^B Y father — chance of colour-blind daughter?
What does it mean for an allele to be 'dominant'?
options: A dominant allele physically destroys the recessive allele in the genome.
A dominant allele is the most common allele in a population.
It is expressed in the phenotype when at least one copy is present (in a heterozygote).
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.

mcqs.q: What does a gene code for?
options: Organisms decide what features they need and grow them by force of will.
Typically a polypeptide (protein) — through transcription to mRNA and translation by ribosomes.
A gene codes for a specific physical feature like eye colour directly.
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.

mcqs.q: How does a population of organisms become better adapted to its environment over time?
options: Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
Organisms decide what features they need and grow them by force of will.
Individual organisms change during their lifetime in response to their environment and pass the changes on to offspring.
Individuals with advantageous heritable variations survive and reproduce more; their alleles increase in frequency over generations.
